newsitem.title: UK: BA faces new strike threat from ground staff.
newsitem.headline: BA faces new strike threat from ground staff.

text.p: British Airways, strike-bound by an acrimonious dispute with cabin crew, faced a fresh threat of industrial action on Thursday when ground staff voted to reject a company proposal to sell its Heathrow airport catering unit.
Ground staff will meet on Monday to decide how the dispute will progress.

The decision by the BA catering staff union -- who voted by a majority of 551 to 178 to reject the proposals -- means BA must now fight a two-pronged assault by its employees who are unhappy over the airline imposing a plan to save one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) in costs by 2000.

The rejection came at the end of the second day of a strike by cabin crew against newly-imposed pay structures and conditions which has grounded hundreds of flights and stranded thousands of passengers since Wednesday morning.

Earlier, reconciliation appeared to inch forward as both management and a union body speaking for the cabin crew agreed the need for talks to end their dispute, the first major strike under Britain's new Labour government.
The Trades Union Congress (TUC), the main umbrella body for British unions, called on BA non-executive directors to use their influence to find a solution.

TUC general secretary John Monks, a moderate unionist, however expressed concern about the "unacceptable way" British Airways had handled the dispute" which, he said, was more about 'union-busting' than about an airline becoming more competitive.
BA's chief executive Bob Ayling, a friend of British Prime Minister Tony Blair, responded immediately by saying he strongly rejected the TUC charge that BA had tried to intimidate its staff.
"My managers have rightly pointed out to our employees the consequences of taking strike action," he said.

BA has warned its employees they face loss of travel perks and opportunities of promotion if they went on strike. It has also threatened to sack or even sue individual strikers -- tactics which the unions have termed "intimidatory" and "macho".

The airline, one of the world's most successful, urged striking cabin crew to reopen talks, but continued to threaten the main transport union with legal action over the legality of its strike ballot.
BA said it expected to see continued improvement in services operating on Friday after it increased its services by 25 percent on Thursday from Wednesday.

However the airline expected disruption to spill over into the weekend before services got back to normal, with only 75 percent of all its longhaul flights likely to operate and 50 percent of shorthaul on Saturday.

As BA turned up the heat on strikers with threats of legal action and of bringing in newly-recruited replacements, it said it had chartered six or seven aircraft and was offering cabin crew free taxis and hotel accommodation to ensure they turned up for work.

George Ryde, the Transport & General Workers Union (T&G) union's senior official, said chartering aircraft would make little difference to the impact of the strike, which he said received "solid support".
The T&G says it will call another 72-hour strike unless agreement is reached with management.

The industrial action is part of a war BA is fighting on several fronts. The carrier is striving to get clearance for a massive alliance with American Airlines, while also fighting off a legal challenge from Laker Airway Inc in Florida.
